One team has used Meilisearch for about six months and is "delighted with its performance and usability." It uses a fraction of Elasticsearch's resources, and language support is extensive and active. Their cluster is small, so they can't speak to reliability at massive scale. They praised active contributors on GitHub and Discord.
A small-site owner considered self-hosting Meilisearch to replace Postgres full-text search. They found the cloud free tier generous but balked that the next plan was $1200/month.

A user was excited to see a non-GC'ed search engine that looked solid. But the replicated/distributed version isn't in the free tier, which makes it hard to really evaluate. Another user noted the free tier lacks high availability.

An Elasticsearch user re-evaluated at 1.0. The .NET client was still alpha, and the engine is very zero-configuration, with no options for tokenization strategies. Meilisearch replicates ~70% of their ES setup with no config, which is impressive, but switching would mean giving up the other 30%.

A team tried Meilisearch for large datasets but found RAM usage impossible to plan. Usage was low with few searches but could exceed what they provisioned under heavy search traffic. This made it too unpredictable and expensive, so they went with Manticore instead.

A user runs the core engine (Milli) as a local indexer over their repositories and Obsidian files: "works like a charm." Indexing is surprisingly fast. The only thing they miss is a typeahead feature.
Another team has used it in production for a few months and is "more than happy with its reliability." They say search speed and especially indexing speed have increased a lot.

An ES user following the project says two things block switching: multi-index search (one type-ahead box across users, companies, tasks) and decay functions for phasing out results by age or distance, which Elasticsearch supports well.

A production user calls it the closest thing to self-hosted Algolia. However, indexing of constantly changing records fell behind for hours: an ecommerce system with 50k changing records "falls over pretty quick," forcing a move to Elastic. The Rails gem also fell out of step with the server. It was great for rarely-changing data, with out-of-box search performance better than Elastic.

A hobby site indexes ~200K small documents with great performance. Pain points:
- Default text matching is too strict, so different word order gives no matches.
- Creating an index, uploading docs and changing settings took almost a week of coding.
- Search can't span multiple document types.
- Default document/upload size limits are too low.
Still: "I love how productive Meilisearch made me."

A user with 15k documents (~70 pages of HTML each) on Elasticsearch/Searchkick tried MeiliSearch for 30 minutes. Indexing was about 10x faster and search at least 3x faster, with literally zero config. It used 140MB RAM, versus ES needing 1–1.5GB to avoid crashing.

Early criticism: only one filter allowed, so search is very fast but limited, "not great for anything remotely complex like searching with two conditions." Another commenter found the single-filter approach restrictive and was leaning toward Manticore Search instead.

Some users objected to analytics being on by default (a daily ping with a unique identifier). They argued it should be opt-in, since it discloses activity and IP addresses. One said this, plus overhyped Elasticsearch-alternative framing, made them dismiss the project.

Heavy Elasticsearch users said MeiliSearch isn't comparable to ES. They need redundant storage of billions of records, time/geo search, Kibana visualizations and horizontal scaling. They called it a nifty tool for search-bar use cases rather than an ES replacement.

One team uses Meilisearch in production with a 7-million-article corpus and says it works really well. They needed a 16GB machine for the initial import because batch indexing is memory-intensive. Afterwards they scaled back to half that RAM and it's "very performant."

A self-hoster runs ~80M documents (191GB, 13 indexes) on a 64GB Hetzner box: "It's bored. Searches are fast." Early on, before batch indexing existed, indexing couldn't keep up and CPU stayed pegged. The team helped via Discord, and later releases plus batch indexing fixed it. "Would recommend Meilisearch."

A user recently tested Meilisearch and called it a great experience. Getting multi-index search running in their frontend was very easy. They wish the cloud had an Australian region, since the closest is Singapore.

Deployment reports:
- One user stood up the server in their k8s cluster easily, especially compared to Elastic.
- Another used Coolify's one-click Docker install and sent 1,000,000 records; it "just worked" on an $8/mo Hetzner instance.

A long-time production user (notado.app) says an older version is "chugging along and doing a great job." They chose it for high-quality multilingual search results. They added that the new AI references "don't inspire confidence at all."
A user checked HuggingFace's Meilisearch-powered search and measured ~360ms for the server response. They questioned whether that matches the advertised "instant search."
